newsitem.title: GERMANY: KJS says committed to German coffee mkt leadership.
newsitem.headline: KJS says committed to German coffee mkt leadership.

text.p: German coffee market leader Kraft Jacobs Suchard (KJS) remains firmly committed to maintaining and expanding its German market leadership in coffee, chairman Bernhard Huber said on Wednesday.

Asked whether KJS might consider reducing or moving coffee roasting capacity in line with ongoing restructuring efforts at the coffee, confectionery and food group, part of Philip Morris Inc., he told a news conference such efforts would focus on areas other than coffee.
Huber said KJS might strengthen the role of its key 150,000 tonnes per year roasting plant,
"It could become interesting in terms of a wider European distribution structure," he said in response to questions.
"For example, we do not have our own plant in Poland, where we are the market-leading roaster."
KJS has another 10,000-20,000 tonnes of roasting capacity at two other sites in Germany, which are mostly operated for decaffeination and instant coffee.
He conceded German coffee consumption had been growing only slowly since the second half of 1996.
It would never expand significantly now that eastern Germany had reached western German per-capita consumption levels.
Profit margins in coffee, as in other foods and beverages, were under pressure amid fierce competition.
KJS in 1996 had improved its post-tax profits to 210 million marks from 120 million in 1995 largely due to the positive effects of restructuring while sales values in all products were down.
Separate coffee tonnages were not available but coffee sales values were down 7.7 percent at 2.2 billion marks.
The company needed to shed more staff and continue to streamline its distribution and logistics.
Nevertheless, drastic changes, perhaps including partial sell-offs, would not be made in coffee, but more likely in food areas such as cheeses or cakes.

Chocolate sales were improving and the company had mastered a difficult period in 1996 when sales declined after the price of its flagship product Milka, a 100 gram solid chocolate bar, were raised by nine percent to 0.95 marks.
The coffee section was pleased with market share gains in its new mild coffee products which were introduced last year.
